rolls_royce.public_statement: Rolls-Royce is funding a further Trent 1000 durability upgrade, starting now. Time on wing is what our customers buy, and it pays back in years, not decades. Do we believe we can win back share on the 787? Absolutely. On UltraFan, the technology is real: the demonstrator has run at full power, and the architecture scales from widebody down to narrowbody. But we don't commit that easily. Airframers need to go there first, and if it is not profitable, we won't do it. When an airframer commits to UltraFan, we will commit with it, and the engine will be mature when the aircraft enters service. This is a milestone on our journey, not our final destination.

disclose: Rolls-Royce has not launched UltraFan this round and will not launch it without a launch customer. If an airframer announces this round an NGSA or fps launch on UltraFan for a named year in 2031-2035, Rolls-Royce will launch the UltraFan narrowbody engine in round 2. For NGSA we launch in the announced year. For fps we launch within the same round, timed so that the engine is ready by the aircraft's own entry into service. The NGSA offer also stands in round 3, for launches up to 2038.

If an airframer announces an A350 Re-engine or a 787 Re-engine on UltraFan for a named year, Rolls-Royce will launch the UltraFan widebody engine one year ahead of that year for 2032 or later, so the aircraft does not wait for us. For a 2031 launch we launch in the same year, and the engine is ready six years after launch.
No UltraFan entry into service earlier than launch plus seven years for the narrowbody engine alone, or six years for the widebody engine or a narrowbody Joint Venture. We do not compress maturity.

Partnership is our preference, not a need. Pratt & Whitney is welcome as a Joint Venture partner on the UltraFan narrowbody. A partner must announce in one round that it will join in the next. Without one, we launch alone.

From the CFO: any UltraFan launch will be funded from operating cash, within our capital allocation framework and against our mid-to-high-teens hurdle rates. We don't have any intent of levering up for it. That's our best view at the minute.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: Pratt & Whitney is controlling what we can control. Time on wing is the name of the game, so we are committing now to put the GTF Advantage hot-section durability into the installed fleet. We have learned our lesson from the earlier versions of the GTF. Our next-generation geared turbofan starts development in 2030 with a full durability programme. It is sole source, on standard terms, and will be ready in 2036. We are not in the early-entry phase. The geared architecture is the architecture of the future, and we intend to be on the next single-aisle cycle. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks. The investment fits inside RTX's existing R&D and capex envelope. The dividend comes first, and our deleveraging path is unchanged.

cfm.public_statement: Our priorities have not changed: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. We are committing the LEAP durability upgrade across the fleet. The LEAP-1A hardware is certified and new engines are at CFM56 time on wing; the 1B follows, and the fixes go in at shop visits, so think years, not months. On supply, you are not going to see us as the finger pointers; you will see us as the problem solvers, with our engineers on supplier floors, and we will pace what we take on to what the supply base can carry. On the next single-aisle, we want to be on all the critical platforms, and we do not have a birthright on that next order. We will earn it with both airframers. RISE remains the most promising path to the 20%-plus fuel-burn step, but when it goes into service is really not for us to say. That is our customers' call. We will tell you what we know and tell you what we don't.

boeing.public_statement: Our priorities haven't changed: safety and quality first, stability in the factory, finishing the 737-7, the 737-10 and the 777X, and paying down debt so we are solidly investment grade. Castings, forgings and skilled labour are tight across the whole industry, so we will not ask our supply chain for more 737 rate until the KPIs tell us it is ready. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early. We're turning it. I don't think it's turned. On a new single-aisle, we will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and it has to be 20% to 30% better than what flies today. A clean-sheet airplane takes longer than this industry likes to assume, so when we commit it will be to a higher confidence plan with schedule and cost protection built in, not to a date we can't keep. We are not announcing any decision dates today. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.

rolls_royce.public_statement: Fuel at these prices makes the case for efficiency, and efficiency is what we sell: the UltraFan technologies are 10% better than the most efficient engine flying today. But we don't commit that easily. Next-generation engines follow next-generation aircraft, and we need airframers to go there first. No airframer has launched an aircraft on UltraFan, and we will not put billions into an engine for an aircraft that does not exist. When we commit, we honour it, and until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing. Narrowbody is an opportunity, not a necessity. If it is not profitable, we won't do it, because we don't need to. Our widebody franchise is performing: the Trent 1000 upgrade is going into the fleet, and we are very aligned with Airbus. disclose: Rolls-Royce did not launch UltraFan in 2031-2035, because no airframer launched or announced an aircraft on it. We do not commit a new engine ahead of a launch customer. We commit in the same round as the airframer that names UltraFan, and a same-round commitment is a formal, binding commitment.

To Boeing: if Boeing launches fps on UltraFan in round 3, Rolls-Royce will formally commit the UltraFan narrowbody engine in that same round, so that it is committed when the selection is made, and timed so the engine is ready for the aircraft's entry into service. Entry into service will be no earlier than launch plus seven years.

If Airbus announces an A350 Re-engine on UltraFan, or Boeing a 787 Re-engine on UltraFan, for a named year from 2036, Rolls-Royce will launch the UltraFan widebody engine in round 3. For a 2037 or later launch, we launch one year ahead, so the aircraft does not wait. For a 2036 launch, we launch in 2036 on terms that leave the aircraft at least as well off as with its alternative engine.

Partnership remains our preference, not a need. Pratt & Whitney's offer to join an UltraFan narrowbody Joint Venture is noted. It applies in any round for which an airframer has disclosed that it will fly UltraFan.

From the CFO: no new engine programme was launched this period, so our capital frame is unchanged: the balance sheet first, then distributions, then disciplined investment against mid-to-high-teens hurdle rates. Any UltraFan launch in the next period will be funded from operating cash. We don't have any intent of levering up for it. That's our best view at the minute.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: Pratt & Whitney is controlling what we can control. We started the next-generation geared turbofan for the next single-aisle cycle. That airplane is now committed to another engine, and no airframer has selected ours, so we are stopping the program now rather than spend into a launch that isn't there. These have to be responsible bets with responsible paybacks. The geared architecture is still the architecture of the future, and we will keep maturing the technology without a launch commitment. Our focus is the GTF fleet: time on wing is the name of the game, the durability upgrade is going into the installed fleet, and we will support every GTF operator for the life of the fleet. We are single-aisle focused. If an airframer commits to a new engine, we are prepared to share the risk and the investment with a partner. The dividend comes first, and our deleveraging path is unchanged.

cfm.public_statement: Our priorities have not changed: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. On LEAP, the durability upgrade we committed is going into the fleet at shop visits, and time on wing is where we said it would be. Think years, not months, and we will keep at it. On the 787, GE is committing a GEnx improvement package for the fleet: more time on wing and better fuel burn for our customers. With fuel where it is, efficiency is worth more to every airline, and every engine we make today runs on approved sustainable aviation fuel. On the next single-aisle, we want to be on all the critical platforms, and we don't have a birthright on that next order. Any airframer that chooses CFM can fly a LEAP derivative on its own schedule, with no wait for us. We commit capital to a new engine alongside a committed airplane, not ahead of one. That is how we earn a fair return, and how our customers get an engine that is ready. RISE remains the most promising path to a 20%-plus step, and when it goes into service is really our customers' call. We will tell you what we know and tell you what we don't.
cfm.rationale: BOARD. NGSA was launched in 2028 on the LEAP derivative (cfm_leap_plus, EIS 2035, capture 1.03) and is locked. It is worth nb_engines +16.82 to us. The only open narrowbody is Boeing's fps. Under the delay its EIS is launch+10 and it waits for nothing. Pratt & Whitney's gtf_next was launched in 2030 on standard terms, is ready in 2036 and has no airframe yet; P&W says it keeps the engine only for an airframer that names pw_gtf2 by the end of this round. Boeing disclosed that it will consider only an engine whose maker commits by 2034 and that is ready by 2041, which points to a 2031 fps. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan only with a launch customer. The closest precedent is the NMA of 2018-19: 'LEAP the baseline ... a half generation' [CX-1126], 'additive' economics with talks kept private [CX-0301][CX-0139], and no CFM engine committed ahead of Boeing. G1 fails (no committed airframer, and Boeing requires readiness by 2041) and G3 fails, so a RISE launch now would break hard rule 2. It gives CFM +8.13 but enters service in 2046. Supply: one commitment this turn, widebody, with strain 0.0 [CX-0993][CX-0556]. boeing.public_statement: Our priorities haven't changed: safety and quality first, and stability in the factory. The 737 line has run stable on the KPIs we agreed with the FAA, so we are taking the next rate step, and we will keep pacing it to what our suppliers can carry. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early. Today we are launching the 787 Re-engine, on an upgraded GE engine, for entry into service in 2036. It is a derivative we know how to build, it keeps the 787 the most efficient airplane in its class, and we are doing it to a higher confidence plan, with schedule and cost protection built in, funded from our operating cash flow. On a new single-aisle, nothing has changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and when the business case works for our customers and for us. We are not going to chase a date. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We're turning it. I don't think it's turned.

Ortberg frames: KPIs stable, no quality/FAA/crunch inject this round, so the rate step is allowed [BX-1271, B-2221]. Boeing's 787 Re-engine entered service in 2036 on schedule on GE's upgraded GEnx. Airbus's Board has shelved the A350 Re-engine it had signalled for 2037, so buyers no longer have a reason to wait: 787 operators and lessors add orders, while A350 customers stay on the Trent XWB. Rolls-Royce launched its UltraFan widebody in 2036, but no airframe has selected it, so airlines treat it as technology, not product. NGSA has been in service since 2035 with no slips and offers LEAP-1A commonality, so A320neo operators line it up for the replacement wave. Boeing chose Do Nothing on a new single-aisle, so MAX customers hold their slots on the rate ladder.
